body:
Why economic development must consider the environment

Economic activities require energy, water, minerals, land and other natural resources. Production and consumption also generate wastes and pollutants. If resources are extracted faster than they can be renewed, or pollution exceeds the environment's capacity to absorb it, economic growth can damage the natural systems on which future production and human well-being depend.

For example, industrial development may increase income and employment while simultaneously reducing groundwater availability or polluting a river. The immediate increase in production does not show the full environmental cost. Sustainable development therefore requires economic progress to be considered together with environmental protection and social well-being.

Meaning of a green economy

A green economy is an economy that is low-carbon, resource-efficient and socially inclusive. It seeks to improve human well-being and social equity while reducing environmental risks and ecological scarcity.

The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) uses these 3 characteristics to explain the green economy. They are connected but represent different concerns.

1. Low-carbon development

Low-carbon development reduces greenhouse gas emissions associated with economic activities. Important approaches include renewable energy, improved energy efficiency, cleaner industrial processes and low-emission transport. Reducing greenhouse gases helps limit climate change, although it does not automatically eliminate other forms of pollution.

2. Resource efficiency

Resource efficiency means obtaining greater useful output or benefit from each unit of material, energy or water consumed. It reduces unnecessary extraction, consumption and waste. For example, repairing a usable machine instead of replacing it can conserve materials and avoid some manufacturing-related environmental impacts.

3. Social inclusion

Social inclusion means that the benefits and opportunities of economic development should be accessible across different sections of society. Green development must consider employment, affordable services, safe working conditions and the livelihoods of people who depend directly on natural resources.

Green economy and sustainable development

Sustainable development is the broader objective of meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It involves economic, social and environmental dimensions.

The green economy is an approach to achieving that objective through changes in investment, production, consumption, infrastructure, employment and public policy. It does not replace sustainable development.

Similarly, green growth generally refers to economic growth pursued while reducing environmental pressures. A green economy has a wider emphasis on resource efficiency, environmental protection and social inclusion.

Growth alone does not establish sustainability

An economy may produce more goods and services while experiencing groundwater depletion, forest degradation or worsening employment conditions. Economic output, environmental conditions and social outcomes must therefore be assessed separately.

Why public policy matters

Many environmental costs are not fully reflected in market prices. A polluting activity may impose health or ecological costs on people who are not involved in the transaction. Such effects are called negative externalities.

Environmental standards, appropriately designed incentives, public investment, research, worker training and better information can help reduce these costs. A green economy therefore involves changes in both public and private economic decisions.

Prelims focus

  • UNEP identifies a green economy as low-carbon, resource-efficient and socially inclusive.
  • Green economy is an approach towards sustainable development, not a replacement for it.
  • Low-carbon development primarily addresses greenhouse gas emissions.
  • Resource efficiency concerns the use of materials, energy and water in relation to useful output.
  • Trap: Economic growth or renewable-energy investment alone does not establish that an economy is socially inclusive or environmentally sustainable.

[References: UNEP, Green Economy, sections on definition, resource efficiency and sustainable development, consulted 1 November 2026; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, Chapter 9, Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11 Economics, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development.]

title: Green Economy: Meaning, Principles and Sustainable Development

body:
How economic activities become greener

Greening an economic activity can involve changing the energy it uses, improving the efficiency of its equipment, reducing waste, preventing pollution or protecting ecosystems. The activity need not belong to a completely new industry. Existing sectors such as agriculture, construction, manufacturing and transport can also become more environmentally sustainable.

A useful distinction is between the environmental purpose of an activity and its actual environmental performance. A technology may be intended to reduce emissions but still require land, energy, minerals and water. Its overall effects depend on how it is produced, operated and disposed of.

Major low-carbon and resource-efficient sectors

SectorPrincipal green activitiesImportant qualification
EnergySolar and wind power; improving electricity-use efficiencyEquipment manufacturing, land use and end-of-life waste also matter.
TransportPublic transport, walking, cycling and electric mobilityOverall emissions depend partly on the electricity source and vehicle production.
BuildingsEfficient lighting, insulation, ventilation and appliancesBoth construction materials and energy used during operation matter.
IndustryEfficient motors, heat recovery, cleaner processes and material reuseEnergy savings must be considered alongside pollution and resource use.
Waste managementWaste prevention, repair, segregation, recycling and compostingWorkers must be protected from hazardous materials and unsafe handling.
Agriculture and waterWater-efficient irrigation, soil conservation and appropriate resource managementResults depend on local water availability, soil conditions and farming practices.
Forests and wetlandsEcosystem protection, restoration and sustainable managementLong-term ecological condition matters, not merely the number of plants planted.

Energy efficiency and resource efficiency are not identical

Energy efficiency measures the useful service obtained from a given quantity of energy. An efficient motor can deliver the same mechanical output while consuming less electricity.

Resource efficiency is broader. It also covers minerals, biomass, soil, water and other materials. An industrial process may consume less electricity but more freshwater. It would be misleading to judge its total environmental performance using electricity consumption alone.

The circular economy

A circular economy seeks to retain the usefulness of products and materials for longer and reduce waste. It contrasts with a predominantly linear pattern in which resources are extracted, made into products, used and discarded.

Important circular practices include reducing unnecessary consumption, extending product life, maintaining and repairing products, reusing components, remanufacturing equipment and recycling materials. Recycling is valuable, but preventing avoidable waste or extending the life of a useful product can often save more resources.

Relative and absolute reductions in environmental pressure

An activity becomes less resource-intensive when it uses fewer resources per unit of output. However, total resource consumption may still rise if production grows sufficiently fast.

Illustrative comparison

Suppose a factory reduces water use per product from 10 litres to 8 litres. If it produces 100 products, water use falls from 1,000 litres to 800 litres. But if production increases to 150 products, total water use becomes 1,200 litres despite the efficiency improvement.

This distinction is central to decoupling. Relative decoupling occurs when environmental pressure grows more slowly than economic activity. Absolute decoupling occurs when environmental pressure declines in absolute terms even as economic activity grows. Efficiency improvements alone do not guarantee absolute decoupling.

A related idea is the rebound effect: efficiency can reduce the cost of using a resource, encouraging additional use that offsets some of the expected savings.

Prelims focus

  • Low-carbon activities aim to reduce greenhouse gas emissions; resource-efficient activities aim to use fewer resources for a given useful result.
  • Green activities can exist in traditional sectors as well as emerging sectors.
  • A circular economy emphasises prevention, continued use, repair, reuse and material recovery.
  • Relative decoupling does not necessarily mean a reduction in total environmental pressure.
  • Trap: A product described as green must still be assessed for its wider environmental impacts.

[References: UNEP, Green Economy, section on sustainable consumption, production and resource efficiency, consulted 1 November 2026; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8 Geography, Chapter 1, Resources; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11 Economics, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development; ILO, What is a green job?, sections on environmental contributions, consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: Low-Carbon Sectors and Resource-Efficient Economic Activities

body:
Meaning of a green job

According to the International Labour Organization (ILO), green jobs are decent jobs that contribute to preserving or restoring the environment. They may occur in traditional sectors or in emerging environmental sectors.

Under this definition, environmental contribution and employment quality are both important. The term does not simply mean any job connected with a renewable-energy company or an environmental project.

How green jobs benefit the environment

The ILO identifies several ways in which work can contribute to environmental protection:

  • Improving energy and raw-material efficiency.
  • Limiting greenhouse gas emissions.
  • Reducing waste and pollution.
  • Protecting or restoring ecosystems.
  • Helping people and communities adapt to the effects of climate change.

For example, workers may install solar panels, repair energy-efficient equipment, maintain wastewater treatment facilities, restore mangrove habitats or improve the efficient use of materials in a factory.

Jobs in green sectors and green tasks in other sectors

There are 2 useful ways to identify environmentally beneficial work.

Green output

Some businesses supply goods or services that directly support environmental objectives. Examples include renewable-electricity generation, environmental restoration services and equipment for controlling pollution.

Greener production processes

Other jobs improve environmental performance within businesses whose final products are not specifically environmental goods. A technician who reduces water losses in a textile factory or an engineer who improves the energy efficiency of industrial machinery performs environmentally beneficial work in a conventional sector.

The distinction matters because the environmental benefit of a company's product does not establish that every process in that company is clean. Equally, a conventional product may be manufactured through processes that use fewer resources and produce less pollution.

Why decent work matters

Decent work includes fair and adequate earnings, safe and healthy working conditions, respect for workers' rights, access to social protection and opportunities for workers to express their concerns through appropriate representation and dialogue.

Consider a person sorting recyclable waste. The work may recover useful materials and reduce waste sent for disposal. However, exposure to hazardous substances, inadequate protective equipment, very low earnings or a lack of basic labour protection can make the employment unsafe or exploitative.

Such work has an environmental contribution, but it does not automatically satisfy the ILO's decent-work requirement for green jobs.

Employment quantity and employment quality

Green investment can create new employment, but the number of jobs and the quality of jobs must be examined separately. A project may create many temporary construction jobs but fewer long-term operation jobs. It may also require skills that existing workers do not possess.

Useful employment indicators include earnings, stability of work, occupational safety, access to training, social protection and participation by women and disadvantaged groups.

There is no single universally applied statistical definition of green employment. Some employment estimates count jobs in environmental industries, while the ILO's policy definition explicitly includes decent work. A reported number of green-sector jobs should therefore not automatically be interpreted as the number of decent green jobs.

Prelims focus

  • The ILO links green jobs with environmental protection or restoration and decent work.
  • Green jobs can occur in manufacturing, construction, agriculture, services and environmental industries.
  • Jobs may contribute through environmentally beneficial products or greener production processes.
  • Safe working conditions, workers' rights and adequate earnings are aspects of decent work.
  • Trap: Employment in a renewable-energy or recycling industry is not automatically decent employment.

[References: ILO, What is a green job?, definition and sections on environmental benefits and production processes, consulted 1 November 2026; ILO, Green Jobs Research Guide, definition and related concepts, consulted 1 November 2026; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11 Economics, Chapter 7, Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues.]
